I looked at the surprise on her face and wondered whether all my careful signals had simply looked like friendship. Had she spent these years beside somebody she trusted, while I kept waiting for her to understand a conversation we were not having? The possibility made my rehearsed certainty falter.

I wanted to ask her to explain every word. Instead, I stood there with the terrible possibility that even an explanation would not give me the past back. Her question was real. The answer I kept hearing beneath it might still be something I was supplying myself.
I thought... I thought you knew. We spent so much time together. Everyone thought we were together already.
I knew we were close. You're important to me. But we never said we were a couple, Aleem.

I wanted to lay out everything I had done. Every journey, every late reply I had stayed awake for, every afternoon arranged around her. It felt like more than friendship, so much more that I had allowed myself to treat us as already together. Hearing the missing agreement spoken aloud made my face burn.

The feelings were real. So were those afternoons. But no amount of remembering them could produce a moment when she had agreed to be my girlfriend. I had taken the meaning those things held for me and quietly written her name beneath it too.
What happens to us now? Can we still be friends?

I'm not ready. I know friends is what we've been, but in my head I kept waiting for something else. I can't just switch that off and come for lunch like nothing happened. I need to be away for a while.

I don't think I can face you right now. Every normal thing would hurt, even you asking about my day. I don't want you to have to watch everything you say around me. I need some distance because I don't know how to do this yet.

If I say yes now, I'll still be hoping. You'd think we were okay and I'd still be waiting for your feelings to change. I can't promise a friendship I don't know how to give you. I'm sorry. I need to step back.

She grew quiet. I had imagined relief after finally speaking, but it was awful watching my words reach her. She was losing a close friend in the same place where I was grieving a relationship we had never had. Neither of us could make the other person's loss smaller.
Okay. I won't push you. Take care of yourself, can?

Afterwards, my hand still moved towards her chat whenever something funny happened. I would compose half a message before remembering. The gap was in lunch, in the hours after class, in reaching home without anybody expecting an update. There was no official anniversary to mourn. My days noticed anyway.

Would earlier have changed anything? Would we have been a couple? I kept returning to those questions as though persistence might make them answerable. Meanwhile, the simplest fact waited without changing: I was single. I had been single beside her too. Now I had to learn how to be alone.

Working life gave my days a different shape. There were names to learn, tasks whose urgency I could not yet judge, and mornings when I arrived early because being lost seemed less embarrassing without an audience. I tried to look settled while checking the same instructions for the third time.

Claire found me in the pantry studying the drinks as if there might be a correct first-week choice. She was Chinese, easy to talk to, and had joined six months before me. That made her recent enough to remember being new and experienced enough to know which cupboard held the decent mugs.
That one leaks. Unless you want coffee on your shirt before your first meeting, take the blue one.
Very useful onboarding. They should have put you in charge.
Six months of experience. Cannot waste it.

She showed me where people usually ate and which questions could safely wait until after lunch. When I looked overwhelmed, she checked in without making a performance of helping. Soon I had things to offer back: a second pair of eyes, a remembered drink order, company when a difficult day ran late.
Do you have five minutes? I need someone to tell me whether this makes sense or I've been looking at it too long.
Those can both be true. Let me see.

Five minutes became a conversation over lunch. Lunch became a message on the way home. She sent me a picture of something ridiculous she had passed; I saved a story from my day because I wanted to hear her laugh at it. Friendship slipped beyond the office without either of us needing to announce it.

I learned to recognise her footsteps when she came into the pantry. Some afternoons she only had time to refill her cup, but we could fit a surprising amount of conversation around the kettle. If one of us had been quiet all morning, the other noticed. Being noticed made the unfamiliar parts of working life feel less lonely.

Outside work, Claire talked more slowly. She would turn her cup round while deciding how to describe something, then say exactly what she meant. I liked that. After all the meanings I had once hunted between somebody else's words, her plainness felt restful. I began wanting to be the person she chose for these conversations.
You know you can stop doing the polite work voice. We're not in a meeting.
This is my normal voice. Very professional person, me.

She laughed into her drink. I watched her try to recover her dignity and felt that familiar warmth spread through an ordinary evening. This time I recognised what I was hoping for. I also knew our religions were different. The difference sat among things we knew about each other, waiting for a conversation I couldn't keep avoiding.

I thought about Jia Wen's question. Earlier had become a word I could trip over even in a new life. With Claire, I would speak before years collected around an assumption. Valentine's Day in 2023 gave me a date to stop postponing it. I chose the words for a question, not a speech about everything I had done.

I still rehearsed. That part had survived every lesson. But this time, when I imagined her answer, I tried to let it be something I hadn't chosen for her. It was easy enough alone in my room. In the morning, seeing a message from her made me hopeful all over again, and I had to start the exercise over.

On 14 February, I could barely follow our ordinary conversation. By the waterfront, couples kept stopping for photographs while we moved aside to let people pass. The date was suddenly embarrassingly obvious. I had chosen a day that said the thing for me, and still needed to say it myself.
Claire, I like you. More than a friend. I wanted to tell you properly and ask whether you could see us being together.
I'm sorry, Aleem. I care about you, but I can't be with you that way. Our religions are different. Being with someone who shares my religion matters to me.

I nodded too quickly. Some part of me had prepared for this answer; preparation did very little when it arrived in her voice. I looked out at the water so I could stop managing my expression for a moment. She let the silence stay instead of filling it with a softer possibility.

Thank you for telling me clearly. It hurts, but I'm glad you didn't leave me guessing. I don't have a very graceful response prepared. Just... I heard you. You don't need to explain it over and over to make me feel better.

Okay. I understand. Can we stand here a bit? I need a minute before I can talk normally again. I'm not waiting for you to say something different. My face just hasn't caught up with the part of me that's trying to be sensible.

I won't ask you to change that for me. I knew religion mattered, but I hoped there might be a way you saw this differently. Now you've told me. I respect it. Give me a little time to get past what I was hoping to hear.

There was no negotiation. I accepted her answer, though disappointment followed me home. For once I did not have to reconstruct a hidden message. She had told me something definite about the future she wanted. The difficult part was learning how to remain beside her without treating that future as a challenge.

The next workday, I reached the pantry and found her making a drink. There was a strange little pause before she asked how I was. I could hear the care in the ordinary question, and the uncertainty about whether ordinary questions were still allowed. I was grateful she had asked anyway.
I'm okay enough for coffee. Maybe not okay enough for a long conversation about feelings before lunch.
Coffee I can manage. The blue mug is free.

We stayed friends. There were careful moments at first, then familiar ones. She still needed somebody to complain to after a frustrating afternoon. I still wanted to tell her things. We found our way back through small exchanges until the confession no longer entered the room ahead of us every time we met.

When she laughed at something I said, I felt relieved before I felt anything else. We could still do this. I could hand her a mug without making an occasion of it, ask about her weekend, tell her I was having a difficult day. I wanted those things to count as evidence that I was managing the friendship properly.
There's a café I want to try. Everybody posts couple photos there, but I just want to know whether the food is actually good. You free this weekend?
As your very objective food research partner, yes.

The place had soft lighting, small tables, and prices that encouraged us to make jokes about the rent. Around us, people leaned close for photographs. Claire handed me her phone and asked for a picture before the food arrived. I took several because she always found something wrong with the first one.
You made the empty chair the main character. I'm over here, thanks.

We laughed, checked the menu, and spent an unhurried afternoon together. Afterwards, she said she was glad she'd had someone to go with. So was I. That became our explanation for other places too: somewhere we wanted to try, something nicer with company. We were friends. We had already settled that.

She took my photograph too, directing me to move my cup because it covered half my face. I complained until she showed me the result. Then we sat shoulder to shoulder over the pictures, choosing which ones to keep. It was a small, lovely thing to do with someone. I carried the feeling home longer than the afternoon lasted.

There were evenings by the water when the city lights broke into long lines around the boats. We walked at the same pace, stopped when one of us noticed something, and talked until we should have gone home. Anybody passing could have mistaken us for a couple. I knew how little that proved now.

I liked the actual person walking beside me: her terrible photographs, her patient questions, the way she remembered a story I had mentioned once. The friendship wasn't an empty consolation. That was what made it so difficult to notice when enjoying her company slipped back into wanting more.

Her answer had not changed. Still, an especially good evening could wake a small, stubborn maybe in me. I didn't say it aloud or ask her to reconsider. I simply let tomorrow remain a little less definite in my head than she had made it in our conversation.

I knew what waited at home: a quiet room and more time to think than I wanted. Here, somebody was asking whether we should get a drink before leaving. I could accept a small kindness tonight without solving the whole future. It was very easy to keep choosing tonight.

We gave each other company, a reason to go somewhere, someone to send the pictures to afterwards. We said the outings came without feelings attached. I could say it convincingly enough. But I still caught myself smiling at her name on my phone in a way I did not smile at everybody else's.

Near the end of an evening, one of us would check the time and groan. We stayed for another few minutes anyway. Then she would wave, turn towards her way home, and leave me with a goodnight that meant exactly what she had said. I tried to keep the evening that simple while I waited for my own journey back.

Time passed like that. I could be happy through a whole meal and feel lonely on the journey back. I had learned to ask the question earlier. I had not learned how quickly closeness could become waiting again, even after an answer. Nobody had promised me anything. The waiting happened quietly inside me.
There's someone I've been getting to know. I wanted to tell you myself. We share the same religion. I think this could become something.

This time there was no overheard conversation, no stranger appearing at the edge of a scene I thought I understood. She told me across a table. I watched her choose the words carefully and wished I could make it easy for her without having to feel them first.
I'm glad you told me. I hope it goes well. Really.

I meant it. I also wanted to go somewhere I could stop holding my expression together. Both things sat inside me while she answered. Later, as that relationship found its place in her life, our habits changed. The invitations grew less frequent. Plans that once started with the two of us began somewhere else.

I could still send her something funny and get a reply. That almost made the change harder to explain to myself. There was no single conversation I could point to and call the ending. I simply stopped assuming she would be free, and began putting the phone down before asking about places we had once said we should visit.

I stayed nearby until there was no longer the same place to stand. There wasn't a second confession or a final argument. Just evenings opening up where her company used to be, and the knowledge that she had found the kind of relationship she had told me she wanted.

At home, I opened a picture from one of our outings. The table, the food, the lighting we had made fun of. I remembered being happy there. Then I locked the phone and sat in the quiet, exhausted by how often happiness had become something I could only visit afterwards.

I had tried speaking quickly. I had tried waiting. I had finally said what I felt and accepted a clear no. Still, I was here again. The room seemed to hold every earlier disappointment at once, until the life I had imagined felt as if it had come down around me.
Maybe that's enough. Maybe I just stop looking for love.

I said it into an empty room. There was no one to challenge me, no new message to interrupt the thought. I wanted to mean it. I wanted the wanting itself to stop, so I could get through a day without feeling that some essential part of my life was missing.

Just when I thought I had nothing left to ask for, a different thought settled in my heart: go to the holy land. It came quietly. No sudden certainty that everything would work out, no explanation for the years behind me. Only a pull towards somewhere I had wanted to go, for reasons deeper than this latest hurt.

By January 2026, I was ready to listen to it. I wanted peace. Blessings. Space for doa, and the chance to bring the things I couldn't explain to God without first arranging them into a story that made me sound stronger than I felt.
Imran, I'm thinking of going for Umrah. Properly thinking about it. Would you come with me?

He was a good friend, the kind who could hear a serious question without immediately covering it with a joke. He asked about the trip, let me explain what I had looked at, and listened when I ran out of practical details and admitted I just needed to go.
Let's look at it together. You don't have to figure out everything by yourself.

That January, we booked the journey. Makkah and Madinah were names I had carried for years; now they were part of a trip I was actually making. I read the confirmation more than once. For the first time in a while, something ahead of me felt possible without depending on whether someone could love me back.

Packing was ordinary enough to steady me. Clothes folded badly, documents checked, the charger I nearly forgot. I kept moving an item from one side of the bag to the other as if there were a perfect arrangement. The hurt was still there, but now my hands had something useful to do around it.

At the airport, Imran stood beside me while I checked my pockets again. Around us, people counted bags and called to family members. I had imagined leaving would feel momentous. Mostly, I felt tired, slightly nervous, and grateful that somebody knew where I was supposed to be.
Passport still there? Good. Come, let's go. One thing at a time.
One thing at a time I can do.

During the journey, I slept unevenly and woke with the old ache still familiar. Then I remembered where we were going. I didn't need to arrive as a repaired version of myself. I could arrive tired, carrying questions, wanting peace without knowing what peace would feel like.

When we arrived in the holy land, I paused with my bag in my hand. Imran waited beside me. The air beyond the doors felt unfamiliar against my face. I was here. After all that thinking about leaving, all those small preparations, I had reached the beginning of this different journey.

I had come for Umrah with a tired heart and very little idea of how to rest it. Now that we were here, I wanted to stop rehearsing everything that had gone wrong. I wanted to pay attention, make space for worship, and understand what I had been carrying for so long.
Come, Aleem. We can put our things down first. You're looking at everything at once.

There were other people to get to know in our tour group. Faces became names, then familiar places to look when somebody called for us. I stood beside Imran and listened, still feeling the strangeness of being so far from my usual days. Then I heard a voice I already knew.
Aleem? Eh. You're in this group also?

Nadiah. For a moment I could only look at her. The same girl from my National Service years, standing among people I had expected to meet for the first time. I had travelled here with the thought of setting my hurt down. One of the people at the centre of it had arrived too.
Nadiah. Yeah. I'm here with my friend. I didn't know you were coming.

She wore a hijab, its edge framing the face that had stayed in my memory through years of trying not to think about it. She smiled at my surprise. I remembered that smile before I could decide what expression to offer back. My body had prepared for something painful; her greeting was simply warm.
I didn't know either. You look so shocked. Say hello properly first, can?
Hello properly. Sorry, my brain needs a bit of time.

She laughed, and something inside me loosened enough for me to laugh too. There were people moving around us, bags in the way, another conversation waiting to include her. We had only a few ordinary minutes. Afterwards, I kept returning to how ordinary they had felt. I hadn't needed to defend myself from her voice.

I sat down with the fact of it once she had moved away. The same Nadiah. I could still picture myself in camp, trying to keep the shock from showing on my face. Yet the person who had just greeted her was older. My own voice had surprised me almost as much as hers: a little awkward, but free of the accusation I had imagined it would carry.

Among the people we began spending time with were Kak Mariam and her husband, Abang Yusuf. Mariam noticed when someone was standing awkwardly at the edge of a conversation. She made space with a small shift of her chair and a wave, as though there had always been a place intended for them.
Aleem, sit lah. There's space here. You and your friend have eaten?
Careful how you answer. If you hesitate, she will decide you haven't.

Mariam gave him a look that seemed to have a whole marriage behind it. He smiled and moved something off the spare seat. I liked being near them. Their kindness asked for very little in return: an answer, a bit of conversation, the chance to make sure we were all right. I stopped feeling like a stranger so quickly.

In Makkah, I tried to let the purpose of the trip settle around me. There was room in a day for things I usually pushed aside. Sometimes I noticed how quickly I reached for my phone whenever a quiet moment opened. I began leaving it in my pocket a little longer, allowing myself to remain where I was.

Nadiah was there too, woven into the ordinary rhythm of the group. We greeted each other. We ended up within the same conversations. Each encounter was small, but the accumulated fear I had attached to seeing her again did not match what happened. I could look up, find her nearby, and feel pleased before I felt anything else.

It was the way she listened that I recognised most. She turned towards the person speaking and waited for the rest of the sentence. When she teased me, her eyes gave the joke away before her mouth did. I began to feel that she had returned to the person I once knew, the person I had loved.

That was how it felt to me. I couldn't measure all the years between us by the sight of her hijab or a few warm conversations. Still, seeing her this way brought back a gentleness I had almost stopped allowing myself to remember. The old hurt no longer arrived every time the memory did.

When we climbed Jabal Nur, there were five of us together at the beginning. I remember the company more clearly than any precise arrangement: voices close enough to answer, people checking their footing, the small negotiations of finding a pace. Nadiah was among us. At first, speaking to her was part of speaking to everyone.

The climb gave our conversation a different rhythm. A few words, then breath. A glance towards the next stretch before looking back at the person beside me. I couldn't fill every silence with something clever even if I wanted to. We kept moving, and the little group gradually stopped moving as one.

I watched the ground more than her face at first. It gave me something practical to concentrate on while the surprise of having her nearby settled. Then she said something I hadn't caught. I turned, asked her to repeat it, and found myself smiling at how easily we could do that. I didn't have to pretend I had heard everything perfectly.

Five became fewer. Somewhere in the ordinary changes of pace and pauses, the others were no longer beside us. When I looked around, it was just Nadiah and me. Nobody had announced that we should be together. I hadn't manoeuvred to make it happen. Yet there she was, close enough to hear me speak without raising my voice.
How did we end up just the two of us?
I was going to ask you. Started with five, right? My counting still okay?

She laughed and caught her breath. We paused where there was room to stand comfortably. For a little while we looked out instead of at each other. I could feel the effort in my legs and hear my own breathing settle. When she asked how I had been, the question had enough space around it for an honest answer.
So, how are you now? Work, life... everything? It's been so long.
I've been tired, honestly. I can do the normal things, go to work, laugh with people. But underneath that, a lot has been sitting there. I wanted some time to breathe properly.
Working already. Some days I think I've got the routine sorted, then I get home and realise I forgot something simple again. Life is okay in many ways. I'm still figuring out the rest.
I wanted peace. That's the simplest way to say it. I had things I kept going over in my head, and I wanted to come here with them. See what I could understand, or finally let go.

She listened without turning the answer into something I needed to defend. Then I asked about her. We exchanged the ordinary outlines of our present lives, pausing to clarify something, smiling when the years between updates became obvious. I found myself listening for what she was saying instead of rehearsing what I would say next.

There were things each of us needed to explain from the beginning. We no longer knew all the people in the other's daily life, or what an ordinary afternoon looked like. That gap could have made me sad. Instead I liked hearing her fill a little of it. The girl I remembered was here, with years of living I hadn't been there to see.
Last time you knew me, so much of my conversation was about camp. You must have been very patient.
You always said civilian conversation was too fast for you. Now working already. Can keep up or not?
Depends. If there are too many questions, I still need advance notice.

We remembered book-ins, the strange way a short weekend used to hold so much, how much conversation we had fitted into the edges of a day. I had kept those memories shut away with the ending for years. Now one of them came back and made me smile. She remembered it too. I hadn't imagined every good thing.

There was no long account of who had hurt whom. We didn't settle the past on that mountain. We talked around familiar details and allowed some of them to be tender again. The air moved against my face while she spoke. I noticed that my shoulders had dropped, and that I was no longer choosing each word to keep myself protected.

Once, we began remembering the same thing at the same time and both stopped to let the other finish. She waved for me to continue. It was such a small gesture, but I felt a sudden affection for the ease of it. For years I had remembered our ending more often than I remembered what it was like simply to talk to her.

When a silence came, I let it stay. I had once been frightened that a conversation ending meant I was becoming less important. Beside her here, I could take a breath without immediately finding a question. After a while she said something small about the climb, and we continued from there. Nothing had been lost in the pause.

Later, I kept thinking about that change from five people to two. Out of everyone in the group, out of all the possible ways a day could unfold, we had been given that stretch of time. I knew how ordinary the explanation might be. It still felt extraordinary to be the person walking beside her again.

Then it happened again at Jabal Rahmah. We were there with the group, and once more I found that the conversation nearest me belonged to Nadiah. We climbed, paused, looked around. The people who had been beside us were elsewhere. I turned towards her with a half-formed question, and saw that she had noticed too.
Again ah?
Apparently we keep choosing the same pace.

I looked back towards where I had last noticed the others, then turned to find her doing much the same thing. We both smiled. It felt like the start of a private joke, something that would need very little explanation if one of us mentioned it later. I caught myself wanting there to be a later in which we could mention it.

I knew the tradition associated with Jabal Rahmah: that Adam and Hawa, Adam and Eve, had met again here after coming down to earth. It was a story I carried about the place. Standing there beside someone I had loved and lost, I felt its meaning come suddenly close to my own life.

Once could be chance. Twice, my hopeful heart whispered, surely meant something. I looked at the space around us, then at her, and wondered whether this was a sign. The thought came with such warmth that I wanted to stay inside it. I had arrived believing love might be finished for me. Now I was wondering about another beginning.

I allowed myself to picture another beginning with her. We were older now. We could speak differently, understand more. The possibility felt lovely before any difficult questions reached it, and for that moment I let myself want it.

Perhaps this was what I needed: her face without the old shock arriving behind it. I wanted to keep the ease of this conversation when we left the mountain, to remember her and still feel able to breathe.
I had been so tired of hoping that I scarcely recognised how good it felt. Perhaps my life still held room for something I hadn't planned. I wanted to remain open to that feeling a little longer.

I kept the thought to myself. Nadiah had made no promise by standing beside me. Around us, other people were having their own conversations, taking their own pauses. I turned back to ours. Whatever the coincidence meant, I wanted to hear the person who was actually here, rather than disappear entirely into the future I could imagine.
You're very quiet suddenly. Tired?
A bit. Also just taking it in. I'm glad we got to talk like this.

She smiled, and we let the conversation find its own pace again. I felt peaceful in her company. That was the part I had never thought to hope for: sitting with the very person I associated with being broken, and finding that I could be at ease. I didn't have to erase her from my life to survive remembering her.

Afterwards, those minutes returned while I was doing other things. I would remember a phrase, the look she gave me, the way neither of us had hurried to fill the quiet. I could feel myself making room for her again. This time, at least, I recognised the movement in my own heart. I knew how much I wanted our closeness to mean something.

As we spoke more during the trip, I began noticing smaller things too. Sometimes an answer would arrive after a hesitation, her expression changing before she found the words. Sometimes a conversation that had been easy would become quieter for a moment. She remained kind. Still, I could feel myself reaching towards something that didn't quite meet me.

I thought I saw longing in those pauses, an attention held somewhere beyond the conversation we were having. The more we interacted, the harder it was to ignore. I could not name what she was thinking about. I only knew the feeling it stirred in me: there might be someone else her heart was still turned towards.

That was my reading of her, unfinished and uncertain. She hadn't offered me a story about another man, and I had no hidden piece of information to examine. I had her warmth, her hesitation, and my own memories. For once I tried to leave those things separate while I worked out what they meant for me.

Sometimes she would come back from one of those quiet moments and ask me to continue what I had been saying. I would, grateful that she wanted to hear it, aware of how quickly gratitude could become hope. I didn't want to punish her for a thought she hadn't shared. I also didn't want to ignore the small uncertainty I felt beside the warmth.

The hope did not disappear simply because I noticed the uncertainty. I could still remember our conversation on Jabal Nur and feel grateful for every minute. I could still think of Jabal Rahmah and wonder. But beneath that wondering, another question had begun to make itself heard: could I keep this peace even if we never became us again?

Madinah came after Makkah. I carried the two climbs with me, the sound of Nadiah laughing, the little hesitations I couldn't explain. I also carried the reason I had made this journey in the first place. Beneath every new possibility was the same tired part of me that had wanted somewhere to put everything down.

Imran stayed easy company. We could walk together without giving each other a report on every thought. Sometimes he pointed something out and I realised I had stopped noticing what was around me. I would look where he was looking, answer him, and come back to the place we had travelled so far to reach.

In Masjidil Nabawi, I found a moment alone. There were other people around, but no one was waiting for me to speak or watching for the right expression on my face. I sat and allowed myself to become still. The quiet did not arrive all at once. My mind kept trying to continue conversations that weren't happening anymore.

I noticed my hands first. They had settled in my lap, yet I was still holding myself as if I needed to be ready for something. My shoulders were tight. I let them lower a little. Around me were small sounds of people shifting, footsteps passing and fading, the life of the mosque continuing while I sat within it.

For so long, whenever I thought about my love life, I began explaining. What I had tried. What I had given. Why the hurt had lasted. I could tell the story in a way that made every disappointment lead neatly to the next. Sitting there, I found I had very little desire to make the account convincing.

I looked down for a while. There was something difficult about admitting how much I still wanted to be loved, after all the times I had said I was done with it. Here I could admit it without somebody telling me to be patient or asking what had happened. I could begin with the wanting itself, and the fact that I didn't know what to do with it anymore.

I made a small doa about love. I cannot give its exact words back to you. What I remember is wanting God to help me with this part of my life: guide me towards what was good, ease what I was carrying, help me find peace with what I could not make happen. It was simple enough to come from somewhere beneath the explanations.

The familiar faces came to mind without lining up into an argument. People I had loved. People I had hoped would love me. The younger versions of myself who had waited beside a phone or travelled home with things they couldn't say. I felt how tired they all were. I was tired of carrying them as if none of those days had ended.

I didn't know what the next part of my life should look like. Even here, with Nadiah close again, I couldn't turn possibility into certainty. I let that be part of what I brought to God. The wanting, the disappointment, the fear that being alone meant something had gone wrong with me. There was no need to tidy it first.

Then a breath left me. A long, unplanned sigh, deeper than the ordinary breaths before it. It felt as if something had come out with it, something I had been keeping pressed inside my chest without knowing how firmly I held it. I remained still, surprised by the space it seemed to leave behind.

I breathed in again. There was room. I could feel the air arrive without the familiar tightness gathering around it. My hands rested where they were. Nothing dramatic happened in the space around me; people continued with their own moments. Inside, I felt an enormous relief, so quiet that I wanted to sit carefully and let it reach the rest of me.

I waited for the ache to gather itself again out of habit. It had accompanied so many quiet moments that its absence felt unfamiliar. A thought of the past crossed my mind and passed through. I didn't need to follow it all the way back. I could remain seated here, aware of where I was, feeling the next breath come as easily as the last.

The memories were still there. I could bring one close and recognise it. But the weight that usually came with it had loosened. I no longer felt caught inside the worst part of each story, bracing for it to happen again. I sat in Masjidil Nabawi and felt free in a way I had almost forgotten was possible.

I had kept the hurt close because loosening my hold on it felt like letting somebody dismiss what happened. Now I could remember it without holding it against every new day. I wanted to live in this one.

So much effort had gone into making myself impossible to overlook. I felt tired just thinking of it. Sitting here, I could stop presenting reasons someone should love me. I could let my hands be empty for a while.

I didn't want to reach every new person already expecting the familiar ending. For once that expectation felt like something I could set beside me. I could meet the next part of my life when it actually arrived.

I stayed a little longer. There was no answer naming who I would marry, no instruction to go back to Nadiah. There was this relief, and it was enough to hold my attention. I had asked for help with love. I began to feel how much of that help could be the freedom to stop being afraid of it.

The old rule about Malay women seemed especially tired now. I had carried it from one disappointment into another life, avoiding people before I knew them. Here, I could feel the resentment beneath that habit letting go. I didn't want it choosing whom I allowed near me anymore. Someone new could be herself when I met her.

I imagined an ordinary introduction, the kind I used to step away from before it went anywhere. I could listen. I could ask a question because I wanted to know the answer. I would not have to begin by placing a stranger beside the people who had hurt me. The thought was small, but I felt how much space it opened in my life.

When I was with Imran again, he looked at me for a moment before speaking. I wondered whether something about the way I stood had changed. I certainly felt it: less effort in my chest, less urgency to resolve every thought before the day could continue. I could hear him without another conversation running underneath.
You okay?
Yeah. I feel lighter. I don't really know how to explain it yet.
No need to explain now. Come. We can walk a bit.

That lightness stayed with me when I saw Nadiah. I still liked the warmth in her greeting. I still knew how quickly one of her smiles could find the affectionate part of me. Forgiving her had not made her a stranger. It had made it possible to see her without needing every encounter to repair the past.

As we continued talking, I recognised the hesitation and longing I had noticed before. A pause, a thought she seemed to follow inward, the feeling that some part of her attention was elsewhere. I took those moments as a sign that her feelings for another man might still be there. It was an impression I formed, never a confession she gave me.

I couldn't know the whole of her heart. I could know that I was starting to lean towards a reunion while sensing she might be leaning elsewhere. That was enough to make me pause. I had lived inside that waiting before. This time I could recognise where my own hope was taking me before I built a life around it.

I wanted us to have another chance; I could admit that quietly to myself. Yet I began to understand that we weren't meant to begin again together. I did not need to press her for a place she hadn't offered. Whatever remained unresolved for her was hers to understand. I could care about her while taking my own next step.

I could answer her warmly, enjoy a conversation, and let it end where it ended. Affection didn't have to become pursuit. I wanted the gentleness we had found again to survive without asking it to promise me more.

I thought of the breath that had left me in the mosque. That relief belonged to this journey even if Nadiah and I never became a couple again. I could carry it forward without carrying another expectation for her.
I knew how to make waiting look like an ordinary friendship. I had done it for years. This time I wanted to let my future stay open, instead of quietly keeping it empty until somebody else was ready.

I made no announcement. There was no farewell conversation for her to answer. The decision belonged in the small things I would do next: stop seeking another moment alone, stop returning to each pause for a possible promise, remain kind when we met. I could step away from pursuing her without making the warmth between us something to regret.

When a conversation finished, I let myself turn back towards the rest of the group. For a moment the old impulse remained: find one more thing to say, keep the opening there a little longer. I noticed it, then allowed the moment to finish. There were other people to speak to and a whole journey around me that I wanted to be present for.

The group still had its familiar places for me. Kak Mariam would catch my eye and ask how I was. Abang Yusuf could turn a small observation into a conversation that wandered pleasantly for a while. I joined them and found I had more attention to give. I wasn't spending every spare moment trying to interpret someone else.
Aleem, come sit with us. Every time I see you standing, I feel like I'm taking your chair.
Kak, you already offered me a seat before I even saw the chair.
Then you had better take it. Very difficult to win this argument.

I sat, smiling before I had found something to say. Their company had become one of the quiet comforts of the trip. There was no particular performance needed from me. I could contribute to the conversation or listen, and remain welcome either way. I liked seeing how often they made room for other people within their ease with each other.

Yusuf would pause to let Mariam add something, then pick up the thread without needing to start again. Sometimes they disagreed about a small detail and laughed when neither would give way. I watched them with a feeling I couldn't have managed at home: pleasure in somebody else's companionship, without immediately measuring the empty space beside me.

I thought about how I had felt before leaving home, alone in my room and almost ready to stop wanting love entirely. Here I was, sitting with people whose kindness had become familiar, feeling able to imagine a future again. I hadn't planned this version of the journey. I was grateful to be inside it.

Mariam turned towards me as our conversation found a pause. There was something she wanted to tell me; I could see it in the way she waited until she had my attention. I settled back in the chair and listened.
Aleem, there's someone I work with. A girl I know. I'd like to introduce you to her.
Her name is Nurulain.

Nurulain. A name I had never attached to a memory, a disappointment, or something I wished I had said differently. I listened to Kak Mariam and felt a small, unfamiliar willingness. I could get to know someone. That was all an introduction needed to mean for now.

When it was time to message her, I made the first move. Moving on had given me room to try again; it hadn't removed every doubt. I still paused over the screen. Then I thought of the trust I had carried home from Umrah. I couldn't know His plans by waiting until I felt completely certain.
Assalamualaikum, Nurul. I'm Aleem. Kak Mariam introduced us. How are you?

She answered, and we began talking. Nothing went dramatically wrong. There were greetings, questions, little exchanges about our days. If you had asked me then, I would have said things were okay. Looking back at how little I gave her to work with, I think she deserved a more generous conversation than okay.
What do you usually do when you're free? Meet your friends?
Sometimes. Depends if everyone's free.

That was the sort of answer I sent. Accurate. Finished. No question travelling back with it. Nurul would find another opening: something about me, something about the people I mentioned. I would answer that too. From my side of the phone, I thought I was allowing things to happen naturally. She was doing most of the happening.

My excuse was familiar to me. If a girl wasn't interested, I didn't want to pour my effort and energy into persuading her. I had done enough waiting beside one-sided conversations. But I had brought that caution into a conversation with someone who kept showing up. I was watching for her interest while doing very little to show my own.

Much later, Nurul told me what she had thought of those early messages. She had wondered whether I was a narcissist. I winced when I heard it. She was describing her first impression of a man who answered questions about himself and scarcely asked about her. I understood how I had given her that impression.
Would you like to meet? We can eat and talk properly.

She initiated our first meeting. Even that small suggestion reached me more deeply than she could have known. Someone wanted to spend time with me enough to ask. I accepted, pleased and still a little careful, and we arranged to eat at Yakiniku. At least there, my replies would have a face and a voice attached to them.

Across the grill, Nurul became more than the person keeping my phone conversation alive. Her smile was bright. I could see when a thought amused her before she said it, and hear the small changes in her voice that a message couldn't carry. We settled opposite each other with beef to grill and plenty we still didn't know.
So. Are you always this quiet, or only when you're texting?
Is my texting that bad?
You answer the question very efficiently.

I laughed, partly because I could hear the space she had politely left after that sentence. The beef sizzled between us. I turned a piece and found it easier to admit my awkwardness with something ordinary to do with my hands. She waited, smiling, and I managed more than the few words I would have sent from home.
I think I hold back at first. I don't want to keep bothering someone if she's not interested. But I can see how that looks from your side.
If I ask you something, you can ask me also. I don't mind answering.

There was nothing difficult about her request. Still, hearing it aloud made me notice how often I had treated a reply as the end of my part. I asked something back. She answered. A detail led to another question, and for a while neither of us needed to search for the next subject. We only had to remember the food.

Once, I stopped halfway through an answer to turn the beef. By the time I looked up, I had lost the rest of the sentence. She reminded me where I had been. I liked that: we could interrupt a conversation to deal with dinner, laugh about it, and find our way back together.

The grill gave us pauses without making them feel empty. We could stop to eat, look down to see what was ready, then return to a sentence. Nurul seemed more at ease as we talked. She would tell me that meeting face to face was much better. I was glad she had given the person behind those dry messages a chance.
I want to say something. When you greet me, or start a conversation... I really appreciate it. It may seem small to you, but it means a lot to me.

I didn't give her my whole history across that table. I simply wanted her to know I noticed. I had grown used to being the one reaching, keeping a thread alive, finding a reason to speak. With Nurul, a conversation could arrive because she had thought of me. It felt like a breath of fresh air.

That was when I first wondered whether she could be the one. The thought arrived quietly while she was still right there, talking to me. I didn't need to turn it into an announcement. I wanted another meal, another conversation, more chances to know the woman who had made this one possible.

Her hello had already changed the shape of an ordinary day. I wanted to remember that feeling when it was my turn to reach for the phone: how good it was to know someone had made a little room for me.
She had given me so many chances to speak. I wanted to know what she would say if I gave her the same room. There was a person across from me, with a whole life I had barely begun to ask about.
I had spent so long trying to become someone another person might choose. Here I could eat, laugh at myself, and finish a thought. I wanted to stay present enough to enjoy that ease with her.

We met again. Then again. The first meeting became something we could refer back to, instead of the only thing we knew about being together. A familiar smile greeted me. Conversation picked up from something we had mentioned before. I began looking forward to her company in the middle of otherwise ordinary days.

Getting to know her didn't happen in one long, revealing conversation. It came in smaller pieces: an answer she expanded because I had asked, a joke I understood more quickly now, a pause I could leave alone. I was still learning to be curious. Sometimes I noticed a question only after I had already started talking about myself again.

I could catch myself and return to what she had been saying. It was a little awkward sometimes. I would ask her to go on, then wait while she found the thread again. But I wanted her to finish. I was beginning to understand how much of a person I could miss while preparing my own next sentence.

And I could still feel a distance between us. We could have a good time together and reach a point where she held something back. I pictured a wall in front of her, though I knew that was my way of describing what I felt. Nurul had her own reasons for being careful. I didn't yet know all of them.

I wanted her to feel safe with me. Wanting it didn't make it happen immediately. I couldn't count our meetings and decide she had been given enough time. So I kept showing up, and tried to leave space around what she wasn't ready to share. The person who had been patient with my dry replies deserved patience from me too.

Then, in our messages, she asked a question that made me sit with the phone for a moment. We had been seeing each other, becoming part of each other's time. She wanted to know where we were going with it.
What's next?

I thought about giving her another reassuring sentence. Instead, I found myself considering something I had never done before. I wanted to meet her parents. I wanted to sit with the people who knew and loved her, let them know who I was, and show her that my interest had a sincere direction.
I'd like to meet your parents, if you're comfortable with that. I'm serious about getting to know you. I would like to know them too.

At the time, I thought I had made my intention clearer. I didn't know that my answer had made her feel even more intimidated. She told me later that it had felt as though I might force my way into her life. I had heard her question as an opening; she still needed to feel that she had room to choose.

Remembering that now, I can understand both sides of the message. I was trying to offer something solid. From where she stood, it was a large step arriving while she was still learning to trust me. Sincerity needed to be felt in the way I treated her, including how I made room for her uncertainty.

We arranged the meeting for after my trip to Kazakhstan. The plan gave us something ahead of us, and some time before it arrived. I wanted the evening to go well. More than that, I wanted us to keep getting to know each other in the days before it. Meeting her parents couldn't do that work for us.
My readiness couldn't decide hers. I could tell her what I hoped for, then leave enough room for an honest answer. I wanted whatever grew between us to be something she could step towards willingly.

I knew how easily a careful reply could make me anxious. I wanted to hear her properly even then. If something felt too much, she should be able to tell me without having to manage my disappointment first.

One serious proposal wasn't the whole of sincerity. There would be another greeting, another question, another chance to remember something she had said. Those were things I could give my attention to now.

I left for Kazakhstan with our conversation still open. Travel made the days different, but she remained someone I wanted to speak to within them. When a quiet moment came, I found myself wondering what her day had been like. This time the thought became a question I actually sent.
How was your day? You mentioned something earlier. How did that go?

It was a small change on the screen. Inside me, it felt larger. I wanted the answer for its own sake. When she replied, I read what she said instead of only feeling relieved that she had replied. There was something to follow up on, something to remember when we next spoke.

I could picture her beyond the conversation with me now: having her own day, dealing with things I wasn't there to see, deciding what she wanted to share. I asked about those things. Sometimes I told her something from the trip, and she asked more. Our messages began to feel like a place we both brought our lives to.

Back at the accommodation, I would sit with a reply a little longer. If I hadn't understood something, I could ask what she meant. I didn't have to offer an immediate solution or turn it into my own similar story. Sometimes she only needed someone to follow what had happened and care enough to hear the rest.
You remembered?
Yes. I wanted to know how it turned out.

Curiosity became the key. I had been so occupied with whether someone would choose me that I could forget to learn who she was. Wanting to know Nurul gave my attention somewhere better to go. I could be interested without demanding a promise in return. I liked discovering how much more there was to talk about.

I told the friends travelling with me that I was seeing someone. Saying it aloud made me smile before I had finished. They were happy for me and wished us all the best. I let myself receive that warmth without immediately adding a warning about everything that might go wrong.

There were still stretches when we were each occupied with our own days. I could leave a message and return to the people around me. Then there would be something from her to read later. I liked that she was becoming part of my life while the rest of it continued around our conversation.

As the trip came to a close, the meeting we had arranged became the next real thing on the calendar. Soon I would be sitting opposite her parents. I thought about what I wanted them to understand. There was no impressive version of myself I needed to invent. I wanted to be clear, respectful, and present.

We met at a restaurant. Her mother had a warm, rounded face; her father was a slim Malay uncle with an easy presence. They were two people curious about the man their daughter was seeing. Standing there before we settled at the table, I felt the importance of it without feeling that I had to hide behind it.
Come, Aleem. Sit. Have you been waiting long?
No, not long. Thank you for meeting me.
So, you've just come back from your trip?

We began there, with something straightforward. I told them about having been away with friends. They asked about me, about work and the shape of my ordinary life. I answered without looking to Nurul to finish every sentence for me. When I needed a moment to think, I took one and continued.

I asked them questions too. As they spoke, I could see Nurul listening to familiar voices from a place that was new to me. I liked being allowed into that little circle. There was more to knowing her than the time we spent alone together. Here were people for whom she had never been a recent introduction.
And how has it been, getting to know Nurul?
Good. I'm happy I met her. She's made a lot of effort to know me. At the beginning my messages were very short, so I think she had quite a difficult job.
At least you know now.

I looked towards her and smiled. A little laughter travelled around the table, and the conversation felt easier afterwards. I could admit something imperfect about myself and remain there. Her parents listened with the ordinary curiosity of people trying to place a new face within the life of someone they loved.
And what are you hoping for, with the two of you?
I'm serious about knowing her. I wanted to meet you because you're part of her life. I hope we can build towards a future together, at a pace we're both comfortable with.

I meant it, and I could hear that in my own voice. I didn't have every future detail ready. I could tell them why I was here. Around that answer, we went on having dinner: listening, eating, asking another question when there was room. The evening had space for everyone at the table.

Nurul would later tell me that seeing me there changed something for her. She saw my confidence, and finally felt the affection behind what I was doing. What had first seemed intimidating began to make sense as sincerity. I was serious about getting to know her and being with her. That was what reached her during the conversation.

I treasure that part of her account because I hadn't been able to see it happening inside her. I had simply tried to speak honestly to two kind people. Later, knowing what the evening had meant to her, I felt grateful that she had let me come, and that we had given each other the time to understand it.

The following weekend, we met again. We sat by the pier near the Kallang River and watched the sunset. Light stretched across the water, shifting as the surface moved. For a while, admiring it together was enough. I was glad to be beside her with no table between us and nowhere our conversation had to arrive.
It's nice here.
Yeah. I'm glad we came.

I began telling her about my past. One part led to another: the times I had hoped too quickly, the times I had stayed too long, the hurt I had carried into the next beginning. She was learning where I had been. I was hearing myself describe it without feeling that I had fallen back into it.

Sometimes I kept hoping even when the answer was already there. I thought if I did enough, or waited long enough, things might change. By the end I was tired of being hurt, but I was also tired of the way I kept living inside that hope.

I told her about being so tired of love that I had almost stopped wanting to try. About going for Umrah, and the relief I found in Masjidil Nabawi. I could still remember the breath leaving me. Sitting beside the river, I paused, surprised that I had brought her all the way into that memory.
Sorry. I didn't realise how much I was going to say.
You can take your time. I'm listening.

I looked at her. There was no need to hurry through the difficult part so we could return to something pleasant. She let me find the next sentence. I had imagined openness as a difficult thing I would one day prepare myself to do. Here I was, already doing it, with someone who wanted to hear me.

For a moment I watched the light on the water instead. I could feel how much I had said, and how calm it was between us afterwards. The stories hadn't made her look at me as though I belonged somewhere else. When I turned back towards her, I still felt welcome beside her.
I'm surprised I'm telling you all this. I didn't come here with a speech prepared. I just started talking, and it felt okay to keep going. That means a lot to me.
Thank you for listening like this. I know some of it is difficult to hear. I'm really grateful I can sit here with you and say it in my own time.
For a long time I kept bringing the same hurt into everything. I feel ready to have something new in my life now. And I'm happy that getting to know you is part of that.

The water kept moving below us. I thought about the timing of her arrival: after I had found some peace, after I had stopped trying to reopen an old ending. I had decided to begin a new book. Then Mariam had turned towards me, and a name I didn't know had entered my life.
I'm really happy you came into my life when you did. After Umrah, I felt like I could begin again. Then I met you. It feels like the pieces have been clicking together.

That was how it felt, sitting there with her. I couldn't explain every part of His plans. I could feel my gratitude for the path that had brought me to this evening: the release, the introduction, her persistence, and our growing willingness to meet each other honestly. I wanted her to know how happy I was that she was here.

I remembered her asking whether we could meet, the questions she had kept finding, the way she had stayed in our first conversation when I barely knew how to help it along. Now I knew more of her, and I wanted to keep knowing her. The words I needed were simple enough to say without rehearsing them.
Nurul, I love you.
I love you too, Aleem.

We confessed our love to each other that evening by the river. I could hear her words without searching them for a smaller meaning, without needing to persuade myself they had happened. The sunset continued around us. Beside me was someone I loved, telling me that she loved me too.

We got engaged. Now we are preparing for our wedding, with things to arrange, decisions to make, and a future that keeps appearing inside ordinary conversations. I used to wonder whether anyone would want to plan a life with me. These days, I find myself discussing the next thing we need to do with Nurul.

The wedding is still ahead of us. So is the marriage we hope to build. There are things we are still learning about each other, and moments when we have to slow down and explain ourselves better. I can be quiet when I need to speak. She can need time when I am ready with an answer.

But we can return to the conversation. I can ask about her day and stay curious about the answer. She can tell me when something feels too much. There is still that bright smile, and the warmth of a greeting I have learned to appreciate. I hope I never let those small things become invisible through familiarity.

When I think of the boy at the beginning of this story, I feel tenderness for him. He wanted love so badly and had so much to learn about giving it. I am still learning. I wish I could let him sit with this ordinary happiness for a moment: being included in someone's plans, and making room for hers.

This is where I will leave the telling, while we are engaged and getting ready for what comes next. Nurul and I have more life ahead than I can put on these pages. I am grateful we get to step towards it together, trusting Him with what we cannot see. And inshallah, it will be a happily ever after.
